DiscoveryScanSourceState.description:

Derived from the job rather than restating it: a leg is still pending only
while its job can still run. A job that failed its last allowed attempt is
left queued by the retry machinery but will never be picked up again, so
reporting it as pending would leave a scan in progress forever.

discovery_source_config_id.description: ID of the config this leg of the scan ran.

DiscoveryScanSourceStatus.title: DiscoveryScanSourceStatus
DiscoveryScanSourceStatus.description:
One config's leg of a scan.

Named per *source* config rather than per job because that is the unit an
operator recognizes - "Splunk prod returned nothing, Bedrock failed auth" -
and it is the unit D-11's run store will record. The job ID is carried so the
logs of a failed leg are one request away.

DiscoveryScanState.title: DiscoveryScanState
DiscoveryScanState.description:
Where a manual scan is as a whole.

A scan is not a job, it is the fan-out of N of them - one per config bound to
the chosen engine. It is complete only once every one of those jobs has
stopped, which is why this has no pass/fail arm: some sources routinely fail
while their siblings succeed, and collapsing that into one verdict throws
away the only part anybody can act on. The per-source statuses carry the
outcome; this says whether they are all in yet.

fields.description: Non-sensitive credential fields. Sensitive values are never returned.

health_details.title: Health Details
health_details.description: Human-readable detail about why the source is in its current health state - the vendor's error text, a rate-limit notice, or whatever the last run had to say. Free text and never parsed: health itself stays an enum so it can be filtered and rendered, and this carries the part of the story an enum cannot. Empty when the state speaks for itself, as a healthy source's does.

last_successful_run_at.title: Last Successful Run At
last_successful_run_at.description: When a scheduled run last completed successfully against this source.

consecutive_failures.title: Consecutive Failures
consecutive_failures.description: How many scheduled runs have failed back to back.

is_enabled.description: Whether scheduled runs may be dispatched against this source. A disabled source keeps its configs and its records - it is paused rather than removed, so re-enabling it resumes collection instead of starting a new source.

is_deleted.title: Is Deleted
is_deleted.description: Whether the source has been deleted. Deleted sources are retained so records already collected keep resolving, and so their evidence can be marked as originating from a deleted source.

deleted_at.title: Deleted At

last_updated_by_user.description: Information for the user who last updated the source.

DiscoverySourceAvailability.title: DiscoverySourceAvailability
DiscoverySourceAvailability.description:
How ready a vendor is for customer use.

Declared by the server so the frontend renders preview gates (for example
Bedrock AgentCore) without hardcoding vendor knowledge.

DiscoverySourceClass.title: DiscoverySourceClass
DiscoverySourceClass.description:
Where a source observes from.

One name for this concept everywhere: UP-4976 called it "source type", the
design docs "source class", earlier API drafts "vantage_point", and D-02
briefly "found_by". Settled as **source class**, matching
``arthur_common.SourceClass`` - found_by reads wrong on a configured source,
which does the record rather than getting found. An inventory column can
still be labelled "Found by"; that is a display string.

This is the configurable subset. ``SourceClass`` also has ``otel`` and
``manual``, which a task's provenance has to name but which nobody
configures, and arthur_common exports exactly this subset as
``DISCOVERY_SOURCE_CLASSES``.

Declared here rather than aliased to ``SourceClass`` because the API must
reject ``otel`` and ``manual`` on a catalog entry: nothing configures those,
so accepting one would create a source no scan could ever run. A test pins
this set against ``DISCOVERY_SOURCE_CLASSES`` so the two cannot drift.

Distinct from a "discovery source type", which is one vendor's catalog entry -
the two words no longer name the same thing.

Choosing a class for a vendor has a downstream consequence worth knowing:
D-02 fixes how a record is graded from the class alone. SIEM records are
``inferred`` - a name lifted from a log field - while cloud and endpoint are
``observed``, a row from a provider's list API or a binary seen on disk. That
is derived per record rather than stored here, so this catalog does not
restate it; a stored copy could only disagree with the record it sits on.

discovery_source_id.description: ID of the parent discovery source.

query.description: Query or filter text in the source's native language. Arthur stores this verbatim and never parses or validates it - only the columns a run returns are contracted. Each record a run produces carries this text back in its provenance, so a record can be explained and reproduced.

schedule_cron.description: Cron expression describing how often the config runs. Standard five-field syntax.

schedule_timezone.description: IANA timezone the cron expression is evaluated in.

lookback_window_seconds.description: How far back each run looks, in seconds. Should comfortably exceed the gap between two scheduled runs.

engine_ids.description: IDs of the engines (data planes) this config runs on. One config can run on several engines across different workspaces.

is_enabled.description: Whether this config is scheduled. Disabling one config stops that query alone: the other configs on the same source keep running, which is the difference between this switch and the source's. Disabling the source pauses every config it backs regardless of this flag.

is_deleted.description: Whether the config has been deleted. Deleted configs are retained.

deleted_at.description: When the config was deleted, if it was.

discovery_source_id.description: ID of the discovery source the config belongs to.

name.description: Name of the config, for logs and run reporting.

vendor.description: Vendor of the parent discovery source, e.g. splunk_enterprise.

query.description: Query text in the vendor's native language, stored and sent verbatim.

query_language.description: Language the query text is written in.

lookback_window_seconds.description: The config's lookback window, in seconds. lookback_hours carries the same window rounded up to whole hours for the engine's window API.

source_fields.description: The discovery source's non-sensitive fields, keyed by field name, as they read at dispatch - e.g. the vendor endpoint to connect to. Never contains a sensitive field. Null on jobs dispatched before sources were snapshotted.

DiscoverySourceConfigSpec.title: DiscoverySourceConfigSpec
DiscoverySourceConfigSpec.description:
One discovery source config, materialized into a scan job at dispatch.

The scheduler snapshots the config into the job rather than handing the
engine an ID to resolve, so a job describes the work it was created for even
after the config is edited or deleted, and so a run stays reproducible: the
query text here is the query that ran.

Credentials are deliberately absent. The engine fetches those live from the
Platform over an authenticated API at execution time (D-05) - a job payload
is persisted, logged and listed, and a secret has no business in one. The
source's non-sensitive fields - where to connect, not how to authenticate -
are snapshotted with the config, because an engine cannot read the discovery
source itself: that takes an organization-level role, and an engine's
account is bound to its workspace.

DiscoverySourceCredentials.title: DiscoverySourceCredentials
DiscoverySourceCredentials.description: A discovery source config's sensitive fields, keyed by field name.

DiscoverySourceTest.description: One Test Connection request, reported per engine.

DiscoverySourceTestEngineResult.title: DiscoverySourceTestEngineResult
DiscoverySourceTestEngineResult.description: One engine's leg of a test.

Succeeded means the query ran and returned - possibly zero rows. Failed means
it did not, or the rows it returned do not satisfy the output contract, or the
job ended without reporting at all; the result or the job logs say which.

DiscoverySourceTestState.title: DiscoverySourceTestState
DiscoverySourceTestState.description:
Whether every engine's leg of a test has reported.

No pass/fail arm, for the reason a scan has none: one engine can reach a
source another cannot, and a single verdict would hide which.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description: Human-readable name for the vendor, spelled the way the product spells it - "AWS Bedrock", not a title-cased "Aws Bedrock". Declared here rather than derived from the enum value on the frontend because no mechanical rule gets every vendor right: acronyms, internal capitals and punctuation all survive in a product name but not in a wire value.

source_class.description: Where sources of this vendor observe from.

availability.description: Whether this vendor is generally available, in preview, or unavailable.

query_language.description: Language a config's query text must be written in for this vendor.

fields.title: Fields
fields.description: Metadata for optional and required discovery source fields.

DiscoverySourceTypeSchema.title: DiscoverySourceTypeSchema
DiscoverySourceTypeSchema.description:
One vendor's entry in the catalog that drives the config UI.

Everything the frontend needs to render this vendor's form: the name to show
for it, its fields with their types and sensitivity, whether the vendor may be
selected at all, and which query language its configs are written in.

name.title: Name
name.description: Name of the discovery source field.

is_optional.title: Is Optional
is_optional.description: If field is optional or required.

d_type.description: Data type of the value stored by the field.

description.title: Description
description.description: Description of the discovery source field.

allowed_values.title: Allowed Values
allowed_values.description: List of allowed values for field. Relevant to enum data type fields.

DiscoverySourceVendor.title: DiscoverySourceVendor
DiscoverySourceVendor.description:
The upstream product a discovery source connects to.

THIS IS THE REGISTRY. D-02 (UP-4974) deliberately does not enumerate vendors:
``DiscoveryAgentCreationSource.vendor`` is a plain ``str``, because nothing in
that package branches on the vendor - observable fields, detection and the
visibility ceiling are all declared per source class - so enumerating it there
would make every new vendor a release of arthur_common plus a repin in three
services. This enum
plus its catalog entry is what a vendor *is*, and the display name and
availability live alongside it.

A value is still a wire value: it lands verbatim in a record's ``vendor``
and in its provenance, in JSONB, in two services. So it is not free text at
this end, and renaming one later is a data migration rather than an edit.

Adding CrowdStrike Falcon once D-20 decides is therefore one member here and
one bootstrap module - and nothing at all in arthur_common.

Values follow ``<platform>_<product>`` mechanically per D-02, rather than
shortest-unambiguous, because the ambiguity is not hypothetical: Jamf ships
Protect alongside Pro, Elastic Fleet is already named in the design docs as a
possible second Elastic source, and Microsoft and Google each ship more than
one product that could become one. Under shortest-unambiguous most of these
would need a later rename, and a rename here breaks the wire.

vendor.title: Vendor
vendor.description: Upstream product this came from, e.g. 'splunk_enterprise', 'jamf_pro', 'aws_bedrock'. FREE TEXT, and deliberately not enumerated here: nothing in this package branches on the vendor -- capability and evidence ceilings are declared per source class -- so enumerating it would make every new vendor a release of this package plus a repin in three services. The registry is app_plane's discovery source type catalog, which is also where the display name lives. Values are `<platform>_<product>`, always, so a vendor shipping a second product that could be a source does not force a rename of the first.

address.description: Where to find this agent again upstream. Required: a discovered agent that cannot be located again is not actionable.

observations.description: What the source could see. Only fields in `observable_fields()` are ever populated by this category.

EndpointAgentCreationSource.title: EndpointAgentCreationSource
EndpointAgentCreationSource.description:
One agent observed on one managed endpoint.

Grain is per (software, device): ``address.instance`` is the device and
``address.resource_id`` the software, because the Discovery list shows a row per
machine.

What it fills comes from three places: the collector's on-disk output, the MDM's
device record, and the collector's catalog.

Where the collector's six output columns land, so none is unaccounted for:

========  =============================================
column    carried as
========  =============================================
kind      ``address.resource_kind``
id        ``address.resource_id``
ver       ``observations.version``
loc       ``observations.install_path``
perms     ``observations.permissions``
extra     nothing -- see below
========  =============================================

``extra`` means a different thing per kind (browser type, image size, deb arch,
unit state, listening address) and a field here means one thing for every source.
The listening address is the one value in it worth its own field eventually.

``scan`` rows must never arrive: that kind marks a branch that could not look, not
an agent that was found.

A one-shot scan sees the machine, not behaviour over time. Anything needing
persistent event capture -- outbound destinations, connection counts -- is out of
reach until osqueryd runs with the audit subsystem, which would put code signing,
notarization and PPPC on the critical path.

model_name.description: Name of the LLM model (e.g., 'gpt-4o', 'claude-3-sonnet'). None for ML evals.

model_provider.description: Provider of the LLM model (e.g., 'openai', 'anthropic', 'azure'). None for ML evals.

instructions.description: Instructions for the llm eval. None for ML evals.

variables.title: Variables
variables.description: List of variable names for the llm eval

tags.title: Tags
tags.description: List of tags for this llm eval version

config.title: EvalConfig
config.description: Eval configuration. LLMBaseConfigSettings for LLM evals; type-specific dict for ML evals.

created_at.title: Created At
created_at.description: Timestamp when the llm eval was created.

deleted_at.title: Deleted At
deleted_at.description: Time that this llm eval was deleted

creation_source.description: The reporting source, its upstream address and what it observed.

external_id.title: External Id
external_id.description: The source's own identifier for this agent, and the canonical identity for the record. Never re-derived or reconciled across sources -- whatever the source returned is what it is.

visibility.description: How much of the agent this source can see. Computed server-side from which fields it could actually fill -- see the source class's ``observable_fields()`` and ``visibility_ceiling()`` -- never a UI heuristic.

last_seen.title: Last Seen
last_seen.description: When the evidence itself was observed.

last_scanned.title: Last Scanned
last_scanned.description: When this source was last read successfully FOR THIS RECORD. Separate from `last_seen` because they fail separately, and per-record because a fleet pull returns records of wildly differing freshness -- Jamf's own reportDate is per device for the same reason, so a run-level timestamp cannot answer 'when did we last actually see this device'. Staleness is derived from this rather than stored: see the class docstring.

first_seen.title: First Seen
first_seen.description: The earliest time this source reported seeing it: the earliest `last_seen` the source has reported. Derived by the Platform as reports arrive and never moved forward; a value sent in a request is ignored. Per-source rather than per-agent: a record can be new to a Splunk source and months old to the endpoint one.

discovered_in_run.title: Discovered In Run
discovered_in_run.description: The scan run that produced this evidence. Meant to be what 'new this scan' derives from -- there is deliberately no 'new' status field to fall out of date. `first_seen` cannot serve for it: it is the source's own sighting, which can predate the scan that first reported the record.

source_id.title: Source Id
source_id.description: The Discovery Source behind this evidence. Per-record because two sources of the same vendor can both report one agent.

Evidence.title: Evidence
Evidence.description:
One source's report of one agent.

An agent can hold SEVERAL of these, from different sources, which is why evidence
is a record rather than a set of fields on the agent: two sources disagree about how
much they know, when they last looked, and whether they are still reporting, and
flattening them would force one of those answers to win arbitrarily.

Deliberately not one score. ``detection`` says how the agent was found and is
derived from the creation source, since the source class fixes it. ``visibility``
says how much of it can be seen and is stored, because it depends on what actually
arrived. ``last_scanned`` says when the source was last read for this record.

THERE IS NO STORED ``is_stale``. Staleness is a function of ``last_scanned``, a
threshold, and the current time, so a stored flag would be wrong the moment time
passed without a write, and would need a sweeper job that exists only because the
flag is stored. The threshold is also not this package's to hold: stale for a Jamf
fleet reporting daily is not stale for a SIEM query running hourly, and the source
config carries the schedule and lookback that decide it. app_plane derives it and
serves it in the response, so it stays out of the UI -- the same principle as
visibility.

EvidenceLevel.title: EvidenceLevel
EvidenceLevel.description:
How much of an agent its sources can see right now, as one word.

Rolled up over every evidence record, whatever a list is filtered to: `full` when
a source that is still reporting sees the whole agent, `limited` when sources are
still reporting but none sees it whole, `stale` when every source has gone quiet.
An agent with no evidence at all reads as limited, not stale -- nothing has gone
quiet, which is what `is_stale` says too. Ordered strongest first, which is what a
sort on it means.

creation_source.description: The reporting source, its upstream address and what it observed.

external_id.title: External Id
external_id.description: The source's own identifier for this agent, and the canonical identity for the record. Never re-derived or reconciled across sources.

source_id.title: Source Id
source_id.description: The Discovery Source behind this evidence. Absent for agents predating discovery, and retained after a source is deleted.

detection.description: How this source knows the agent is there -- observed directly, or inferred from indirect evidence. Fixed by the source class. None for manual tasks, which are not records.

visibility.description: How much of the agent this source can see. Computed server-side from which fields it could actually fill, never a UI heuristic.

is_stale.title: Is Stale
is_stale.description: Whether this source has gone quiet -- `last_scanned` is older than the freshness window for its discovery source. Derived on read rather than stored: a stored flag is wrong the moment time passes without a write. Independent of `detection` and `visibility`, so an expiring credential does not downgrade what the source was able to see.

last_seen.title: Last Seen

EvidenceResponse.title: EvidenceResponse
EvidenceResponse.description:
One source's report of one agent, as the API serves it.

Declared standalone rather than as a subclass of `arthur_common`'s `Evidence`, and
with `detection` as a plain field rather than the computed one it carries. The reason
is FastAPI's `separate_input_output_schemas`: a model with computed fields is emitted
as a separate `-Input`/`-Output` pair, and a model nested inside another does not get
the Output variant -- so every list endpoint's generated client would have silently
dropped the computed fields. The values are still derived rather than accepted; the
derivation just moved into the translator, which is the one place that builds these.

The three axes a record is graded on are separate fields on purpose. `detection`
says how the agent was found, `visibility` how much of it can be seen, and
`is_stale` whether the source is still reporting. Collapsing any pair loses
something: an osquery-confirmed binary ranks below a name lifted from a log field on
a single band, and a Traced record stops being Traced the moment its credential
expires.

RunsOn.title: RunsOn
RunsOn.description:
Where the machine hosting a discovered agent is. ONE AXIS: location.

Lives on Provenance rather than being derived from the source type: a Jamf record
runs on a laptop, not on the cloud hosting the engine that reported it.

Deliberately NOT a place for `docker` or `kubernetes`. Those answer a different
question -- how the agent is packaged on the machine -- and mixing the two makes
the common case lossy: an agent in an EKS pod is both `aws` and orchestrated, and
one field can only say one. They are also values nothing can currently fill. In the
endpoint collector Docker is a detection ROUTE (`docker_images`, surfaced as
``resource_kind=image``), and in app_plane `Infrastructure.Docker` describes how
the ENGINE was deployed. Neither is a statement about where a discovered agent
runs. If the packaging axis starts mattering, it wants its own field.

``on_prem`` is the natural next member on this axis and is left out only because
nothing in v1 can fill it: on-prem records arrive through a SIEM, which cannot see
the machine, so UNKNOWN is already the honest answer there.

vendor.title: Vendor
vendor.description: Upstream product this came from, e.g. 'splunk_enterprise', 'jamf_pro', 'aws_bedrock'. FREE TEXT, and deliberately not enumerated here: nothing in this package branches on the vendor -- capability and evidence ceilings are declared per source class -- so enumerating it would make every new vendor a release of this package plus a repin in three services. The registry is app_plane's discovery source type catalog, which is also where the display name lives. Values are `<platform>_<product>`, always, so a vendor shipping a second product that could be a source does not force a rename of the first.

address.description: Where to find this agent again upstream. Required: a discovered agent that cannot be located again is not actionable.

observations.description: What the source could see. Only fields in `observable_fields()` are ever populated by this category.

SIEMAgentCreationSource.title: SIEMAgentCreationSource
SIEMAgentCreationSource.description:
An agent surfaced by a query against the customer's security stack.

One variant for all three SIEMs, discriminated by ``siem``: the payload is
identical in every case and only the query language differs, which belongs to the
connector that runs the query.

HOW MUCH IT OBSERVES DEPENDS ON WHAT THE CUSTOMER INDEXES, not on the vendor. A
query over proxy or DNS logs sees a destination and little else, which is what
every v1 example query does. One over host-enriched data can carry the OS and the
cloud -- ECS has ``host.os.platform``, ``host.os.version`` and ``cloud.provider``;
Sentinel's Heartbeat table has ``OSName`` and ``ComputerEnvironment``. Since the
customer's own query controls the output columns, either is reachable.

OBSERVABLE_FIELDS below is therefore a ceiling in the fullest sense: it says what a
SIEM query *can* project, and most will project almost none of it.

SourceAddress.title: SourceAddress
SourceAddress.description:
How to find a discovered agent again in the system that reported it.

One shape for every source, widest to narrowest:

==============  ================  ==================  ==========  ============
source          instance          scope               kind        resource_id
==============  ================  ==================  ==========  ============
Bedrock         AWS account       region              --          agent id
Vertex          GCP project       region              --          engine id
Splunk          instance          index+sourcetype    --          record id
Sentinel        LA workspace      table               --          record id
Elastic         deployment        data stream         --          record id
Jamf / osquery  device key        --                  npm, app…   software key
==============  ================  ==================  ==========  ============

Only endpoints fill ``resource_kind``: they are the one source whose ids come from
several namespaces at once. Every cloud and SIEM vendor addresses exactly one kind
of resource, so the kind is implied by the vendor and stays absent.

``scope`` carries two readings this one name does not separate. For a cloud source
it addresses the *agent*: us-east-1 and us-west-2 hold different agents, so
``CloudAgentCreationSource`` requires it. For a SIEM it addresses the *sighting*,
and one agent may surface under two indexes, so it stays optional there. Code
comparing addresses across sources has to read `source_class` to know which it is
looking at.

Reused by Provenance rather than re-declared there, so a record and the task it
resolves to address the upstream system identically. A vendor needing to address a
sub-resource -- a Bedrock alias, a Vertex version -- is one more optional field
here, not a new shape.

SourceClass.description:
Where a source observes from. One name for this concept everywhere.

The design docs' "source class"; earlier API drafts called it ``vantage_point``.
Used on a configured discovery source and on a task's provenance alike, so the two
are the same vocabulary rather than two that have to be reconciled.

Consumers branch on this -- capability and evidence ceilings are declared per class
-- which is why it is a closed enum while the vendor is not.

Visibility.title: Visibility
Visibility.description:
How much of the agent the source can actually see.

Independent of Detection: a certain detection can carry almost no depth, which is
the normal case for an endpoint scan, and is exactly the pairing the old single
band could not express.

Staleness is NOT a member; it is a separate ``is_stale`` flag on the evidence
record, so full visibility does not become limited when a credential expires.
